title: Topological building blocks of nonequilibrium response
abstract: Nonequilibrium systems can exploit energy to amplify their sensitivity to external stimuli, allowing them to be harnessed for a variety of functions in both engineered devices and living organisms. An assortment of theoretical results capture different facets of this nonequilibrium amplification, including fluctuation-response relations as well as bounds and constraints that limit the potential behavior. Here, we take a broader perspective, aiming for a systematic characterization of the full range of possible response behaviors. For a wide class of nonequilibrium dynamics, we identify a collection of optimally sensitive models whose behavior is determined by the topology of the state space. We further conjecture that every response can be written as a convex combination of these optimal models, thereby structuring the entire space of responses. We use this geometric perspective to put sensitivity limits on nonmonotonic biochemical input-output functions, and identify all optimal kinetic schemes for the unordered binding of molecules among three sites.
summary: The paper develops a geometric framework to map the entire space of possible non-equilibrium responses in Markov jump processes. It shows that these responses are constrained by the topology of the underlying state graph via 'uniquely constructable' tree families. This provides powerful, mathematically rigorous bounds for designing systems with specific sensitivity profiles.
main_problem: To systematically characterize the full range of possible non-equilibrium response behaviors achievable by a system, moving beyond existing theoretical bounds.
main_result: The entire space of achievable responses is conjectured to be structured as a polytope whose vertices are determined by 'uniquely-constructable' tree families derived from the graph topology.
method: The authors use graph theory (rooted spanning trees) and geometric arguments, showing that physical realizability restricts the response space to a convex combination of contributions from these unique topological structures.
model_or_system: The system is modeled as a continuous-time Markov jump process on a graph G with N nodes. The dynamics are governed by a master equation, and the focus is on calculating the rate sensitivity ($\partial_\lambda \langle Q angle$) of steady-state observables to external control parameters $\lambda$.
key_observables: Steady-state distribution ($\pi_j$), response sensitivity vector components ($\partial_\lambda \ln \pi_j$), and the expected value of an observable $\langle Q angle$.
important_parameters: The topology of the graph G, kinetic rates $W_{ij}$, and the control parameter $\lambda$ that tunes the rates.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the graph is strongly connected to ensure a unique steady state. Crucially, it distinguishes between 'multi-constructable' (non-physical) and 'uniquely-constructable' tree families.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the construction of different types of rooted spanning trees on small graphs (like 3 states), contrasting those that are uniquely constructible (leading to nested or twisted hysteresis motifs) versus those that fail due to structural contradictions.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from defining the general problem of response characterization, establishing the role of tree families in bounding the response space via convex combinations, and finally applying these topological constraints to specific physical models like molecular binding on a 3-state graph.
why_interesting: This work provides deep mathematical structure (polytope geometry) to non-equilibrium dynamics, offering rigorous bounds on how systems can respond to external stimuli, which is highly relevant for designing synthetic biological or engineered quantum devices.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Some example tree families of the 3 state graph. A) Two distinct tree families with trees rooted at the top (blue), left (orange), and right (green) states. The number of times each directed edge is used is given by the black graph to the right. Since both sets use the same collection of edges with the same multiplicities, they can each be reconstructed into the other and are thus mulit-constructable. B) Another pos- sible tree family with its edge multiplicities. In this case, no other construction is possible, thus making this set uniquely constructable.

This process of drawing new values of Q, W, and d and recalculating ˆS(λ) is repeated a total of 4096 times for each network. This data shows the validity of the bounds presented in (8).

FIG. 2. Numeric exploration of response in the 3 state graph. The response of this system exists within a 2-dimensional sub- space of the 3-dimensional space defined by ∂λ ln πj. Axes represent an orthonormal basis of this subspace for each pa- rameter set. The position of the tree family vertices (vσ) are given by the × markers with multi-constructable tree families in black and uniquely-constructable ones in red.
